utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think what we'll do is after we've heard everything the Prosecution has to say, if we could have a break at that point and consider our position. Just three other housekeeping matters. The second is, of course, the Prosecution has produced a chart which we will be discussing today. We also produced a chart to explain our position but my submission would be that these should not become exhibits. I don't know if it will be proposed, but at this stage, this late stage these would be, I understand, as I understand for information only, otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hadn't intended to receive these as submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I assure you we don't take anything for granted. Not even the least reference in any of the final briefs. Each reference is checked and re-checked and re-checked to make sure that we are being given the right information by both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. I'm obliged to Your Honour for that. Just two very short remarks on the exhibits which have been mentioned. P570, we would object to -- to any new pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is. But P598, Your Honour, our understanding is that this is not P598.1, that it's not an exhibit at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not yet, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then that's -- Your Honour, I say that for this reason, that we didn't address P598.1 even in our closing submissions on the principle that it is not even an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the records but we promised you we'll decide on whether it will come in the records as a substitute for 598 or not in due course as we elaborate the judgement. That is part of the decision that we will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because perhaps it's a matter which needs clarifying because when you have this 1. Limitation, sometimes that signifies that it's a subsequent version of an exhibit. utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Sorry. It's simply I just wanted to make it crystal clear on the record that from our point of view we would be prejudiced if 598.1 were used as any part of the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further remarks? None? I thank you. So Ms. Sellers, before I give you the floor because the documents I had before I came in, I seem to have completely -- completely mislaid. utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. I believe I'll take much less time than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be our pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would now take the opportunity to reply to the Defence closing arguments. We would like to reply in the following manner. I will speak first about several legal issues that have been raised by the Defence. Then Mr. Gramsci di Fazio will address you on issues pertaining to documents, including some of the questions that Your Honours have asked us to address. Mr. Di Fazio will also speak to you about sentencing in reply to what was raised. I understand the sentencing part will probably go first and then Ms. Richardson will respond to questions that Your Honours have put before us and I will conclude with one or two other legal points, and then just a very brief conclusion. Again we thank you for this opportunity. We look at our submissions as a reply. The first issue that the Defence raised that the Prosecution would like to address quite briefly is the notion of levee en masse. The Defence appears to continue to characterise what happened in terms of the armed forces of Srebrenica throughout 1992, 1993, and if the Prosecution has understood, even after March of 1993, as a levee en masse. The Prosecution merely states that the definition of levee en masse that the Defence advanced is the correct definition. It does not apply to the factual situation in Srebrenica. The Prosecution's point has been that since the 20th of May 1992, at the Bajramovici meeting when organisation and in particular when command structures were set forth, that any characterisation of a levee en masse dissipated. The Prosecution reiterates the points that were brought up but would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to the accepted fact or stipulated fact that the Defence referred to. They said that they had 40 accepted or stipulated facts within this trial. One of those facts is that Naser Oric was appointed the command ore of the joint armed forces of the subregion Srebrenica in early November 1992. That comes directly out of the indictment and the Defence is correct, that is one of the points that they have stipulated to. By their very own admission of that fact, a levee en masse, in the very least, stopped on November 1992 because command was accepted. Your Honour in the real world, even in the real world of Srebrenica, command was structured and accepted much earlier, and forces started to organise. Levee en masse is inapplicable to our situation and the only reason that the Defence would want to continue to have a levee en masse characterisation is that it goes to questions of the organisation of the forces, the superior responsibility of Mr. Oric and, hence, his responsibility for subordinates. Next I would just like to address the issue of command responsibility. The Defence gave us a definition of command responsibility yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. Let's see if it works now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The Defence gave us a definition of command responsibility that the Prosecution would say is not the definition or the elements that this Tribunal recognises. The Defence argued or advanced to Your Honours that command responsibility entails four elements, that there exist a spear-subordinate relationship, that the accused knew or had reason to know that his subordinates were about to commit crimes or had done so, the accused failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish, and then the Defence added a fourth element: The accused's negligence was so serious as to amount to malicious intent. Your Honours, that is not the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The Defence stated to Your Honours what is a misconstruction of the elements here. That misconstruction will mislead you in your judgement. Negligence so serious as to amount to malicious intent was considered by this Tribunal in the very early days and discarded. Negligence so serious to arise to malicious intent relates to not the standard that we recognise, that the accused knew or had reason to know, but a standard that had been debated within the formulation of additional protocol 1 and the commentaries that speak to it. It relates to the should-have-known standard. The should-have-known standard that I believe that the Defence cited or thought of erroneously as being or had reason to know standard is a standard that does and could possibly lead to strict liability, exactly the concerns that the Defence raised. This Tribunal from the Celebici appeals decision to the Blaskic appeals decision has set forth the elements of knew or had reason to know. As a matter of fact, it's a higher standard, Your Honours, and it's a standard that the Prosecution has met in this case against Naser Oric. Naser Oric knew and certainly had reason to know, of the burning, the killings, the murders, and the mistreatment of prisoners. Article 7(3) is not a liability based upon negligence under our jurisprudence. The Prosecution would just ask Your Honours not to be misled and to apply the elements that have been recognised both in Celebici and Blaskic appeals decisions. The Prosecution would now just briefly go back to Article 7(3), and aiding and abetting within the contents of Article 7(3). Now the Defence would have us dance with the Prince of Wales eventually, but Your Honours it's a very clear matter of understanding the word "commit" and understanding the responsibility of a superior. A superior is not allowed to walk away and said my subordinates, they only aided and abetted, my goodness, I think they only instigated. I think there has probably been a little bit of conspiracy but no commission of a crime. A policy, the underriding policy of humanitarian law is that superiors who know or had reason to know, are responsible if they failed to prevent or failed to punish the crimes. Now, the Defence had a very nice triangle where they tried to show that the superior would have to be over the opportunistic perpetrators and the superior would have to be over the subordinates. Well, Your Honours, I would ask you not to look at the triangle but it's actually an L. The superior is over the subordinates under effective control. Whether those subordinates commit or whether the bottom half of the L reaches out and they in some other manner assist, facilitate, the other perpetrator. I would not want the Defence to neither misconstrue, misstate or mislead Your Honours on that point. The Prosecution has made it very clear that the acts, the criminal acts, that have occurred in Srebrenica in 1992 and 1993 for which Naser Oric has been charged at times were committed by his subordinates, at times his subordinates aided and abetted others, such as in the first prison scenario, such as in the second prison scenario and also in the villages Fakovici, Bjelovac and Kravica in particular. Your Honour, our 7(3) position as it relates to aiding and abetting is a fallback position. It's a position that says that the soldiers indeed did commit burning. Naser Oric's subordinates indeed did commit the mistreatment and the killings in the prison and if Your Honours also see that they aided and abetted, facilitated either before or after, that this liability, indirect responsibility, inures to Naser Oric. Your Honours have asked a specific question in terms of the facts related to aiding and abetting. In Rakovici we have stated that soldiers have burned, as we did in Jezestica. The Defence has put forward the theories that there were civilians and, of course, the Prosecution has never said that the civilians themselves were subordinate to Naser Oric. That is not our evidence. That's not our theory, that is not our case. But whether those subordinates in particular those soldiers from the different units, do aid and abet those civilians, the L reverts back up to Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you here, this precisely is one of the things that I meant to ask you today. According to your thesis, your case, how did the -- the ones you consider to be Naser Oric's subordinates aid and abet the civilians who may have burnt down or destroyed property?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What are you basing it upon?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour we are basing it upon the facts that Naser Oric would go in, and it's not the attack itself, it's the wanton destruction that's committed by allowing the civilians to go in, to burn after they've cleaned out an area, encouraging the burning, under aiding and abetting. In addition to the burning together, Mr. Di Fazio has reminded me. Under aiding and abetting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: As regards the presence of Naser Oric or the alleged presence of Naser Oric, just, I can understand. What I'm referring to is the soldiers because Naser Oric, at least from what I could gather, you don't have evidence to prove that in each and every one of the attacks, Naser Oric was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We haven't alleged that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically I think you need to draw the distinction first of all. So if we speak only of the -- what you consider to be subordinates of Naser Oric, within a context of aiding and abet, if you do consider then -- how do you configure this.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we configure this in the following manner. The presence of the soldiers is not a mere presence. It's a substantial contribution, that they are allowing the civilians to carry out the destruction, whether it's the setting of fire. Their presence as soldiers after having taken it is an encouraging presence. In addition to that when they are participating in other forms of wanton destruction while civilians are burning, that also is an encouraging presence, a substantial contribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And if Oric wasn't there on any one of these occasions, how is he supposed to have known?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: How was he supposed to have known?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, based on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, know -- know that his subordinates aided and abetted the civilians? Your Honour, I think that when one is even back in command headquarters, and understands that the villages that is attacked has been wantonly destroyed or burnt down that is inquiry notice. He does return to villages that have been destroyed. And that's the inquiry notice that in the very least would say, something has gone on beyond going for the military object within the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Sorry for interrupting you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, in conclusion, our 7(3) case as it relates to subordinates of Naser Oric for attacks and for the guards within the prison, does not consider that Naser Oric is a superior over the civilians. I would like to also correct that the Defence had the mistaken impression that the Prosecution was somehow forwarding a 7(1) aiding and abetting theory in relation to the prisons. That is not at all our Prosecution case nor theory. I wanted to state that on the record, Your Honour. Your Honour, at this time, I'm going to ask Mr. Gramsci di Fazio to make his submissions and then I'll return to you at the end of the presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One further question, Ms. Sellers, before we close on this. Yesterday, one of the submissions by the Defence in relation to aiding and abetting is that acceptance so far as it is indicated in count 5, if I remember well, that in relation to Oric's presence and aiding and abetting that where it is not specifically pleaded in the indictment, it should not be a valid argument now in an oblique fashion. In other words, he was not there, but he had inquiry notice just the same or he must have had inquiry notice. The subordinates even when they did not commit any crimes themselves did, however, they are responsible for aiding and abetting. Therefore Oric is also answerable for aiding and abetting or for 7(3) responsibility. This is the question that I have: Where do you see it pleaded in counts 1, 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in counts 1 and 2 that pertain to the murder and the cruel treatment the Defence has been put on notice ever since our indictment. We speak about guards and others coming into the prison to beat. We have also included in our pre-trial brief it's the same factual description that they have been put on notice. The evidence came out at trial. The evidence came out at trial, in particular in the first prison scenario, that others came into the jail, the turnkey opened the door, Cude opened the door several times with the Mrki and Kemo. We also pleaded it within our closing brief. Now they're factual pleadings but within the factual pleadings we believe the Defence has been placed on sufficient notice that their subordinates of Naser Oric aided and abetted other wise facilitated the crimes of others. At times of other subordinates. But also civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not pursue this matter from this point onwards because obviously it becomes tricky but I wish the Defence to address this point a little bit further in your response either now or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I must say I'm deeply confused now and I would appreciate clarification from the Prosecution. Are they saying that our client is responsible for others who came from outside the prison or not? They are completely unclear on that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The purpose of my question very simply put is the following, Mr. Jones: That one of the basic principles of due process and of a fair trial is that the accused must know before the trial starts what he is supposed to -- what charges he's supposed to answer. There is no point in saying that at some point in time in the course of the trial, new, fresh charge or accusation comes to light, and therefore he's given due notice of it, therefore he's answerable, therefore he has sufficient -- it has been sufficiently plead, therefore it forms part of the indictment even if it's -- does not show up in the indictment. What I have asked you is, basing yourself on the submissions made by Mr. Jones or Ms. Vidovic I don't know who, yesterday or the day before, where in the indictment do you see aiding and abetting being attributed as a charge, as a liability, vis-a-vis Mr. Oric in counts 1, 2 and 3? Not in count 5 because in count 5 it's clear enough. In counts 1, 2, and 3. I'm not contesting you anything. Don't misunderstand us. When we put questions it's not because we are --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: It's on the record, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not because we already have a -- that we have decided or anything but these are obviously some legal questions of some interest to us and, I mean, when the matter was raised yesterday, it needed to be, of course, dealt with -- yes, do you want to put a question? Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: May I just make a remark with regard to clarification? I think it is necessary to distinguish between responsibility of the accused on 7(3) and the responsibility of the subordinates. Now, if I understand, and my question is to both parties, if I understand the Defence's submission yesterday, when you had this triangle, you thought of having a direct -- you were discussing and rejecting a direct responsibility of the accused versus the civilians under 7(3). Now, today we heard that from the Prosecution side, it's different. It only refers to 7(3) with regard to the subordinates and the subordinates' responsibility with regard to civilians. And the question as concerns aiding and abetting does only concern the relationship between the subordinates and the civilians and not the relationship between the accused and subordinates with regard to the relationship between the accused, through the vertical line, and the subordinates, there is no change at all. There is -- you -- the law requires the same problems with regard to having superior-subordinate relationship, with regard to knowing or have reason to know and with regard to take measures to prevent. If there is still some misunderstanding between the parties, I would be interested -- or we would be interested to hear about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I make one point, Your Honour? I think we the Defence are entitled to clarity on this point above all else. In that triangle we referred not to civilians, remember, but to opportunistic visitors, referring to the prison. Now we are referring there to unidentified persons who came into the prison, allegedly, and mistreated detainees. Now, what we wish to have clarification on now, because it is now to us completely unclear is, is the Prosecution saying that our client has command responsibility over unidentified perpetrators who came into the prison? I would appreciate the Prosecution to say that because they referred to "others," others who came in and allegedly our client is responsible for those others. If the Prosecution is prepared to say right now, categorically, your client is not charged with any responsibility for opportunistic visitors, these other people who came into the prison, then that would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor is prepared to say, Your Honour, that in the description that I have is exactly as Judge Agius has just described it. Where the difference comes in, the Prosecutor certainly would say, in the first prison scenario, Kemo, we can either go straight down to Kemo with regard to 7(3) responsibility. That is our evidence, that is our thesis. Or we can go in that exceptional case over to Kemo because he's aided and abetted by a guard who also falls under Naser Oric. But what we are talking about and I think what the Defence wanted to have clarified is that we have removed that third part of the triangle. We are not saying Naser Oric has superior-subordinate responsibility for what the Defence calls opportunistic visitors. It is possible, if they are also his subordinates, then the triangle emanates that way, Your Honours. I don't know my geometry but I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. I think it's clear enough. Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just give me a moment to gather my papers? Ms. Sellers moved them around. If Your Honours please I want to deal with the issue of sentencing first. Before I do, before I turn to the main substance of my submission, there is a matter that I need to raise with you that arises from matters that the Defence have put to you in the last two days concerning sentencing. It doesn't go to substance of the doing at hand but rather the expressions used by this Defence. If Your Honours please, there was a portent of things to come in the Defence reply when the Defence referred to the Prosecution submission that a sentence of 18 years was appropriate as being grotesque. The Prosecution had chosen to ignore that particular comment in the Defence reply but matters did not lie there and yesterday submissions were made to you, if I just might remind you of some of the express that is were used, that this Prosecution considers the -- that sorry the Defence considers the Prosecution submissions on sentence a cold-hearted demand, a Draconian sentence, and expressions to the effect that the world will trust, will judge the credibility of the Prosecutor, Ms. Carla Del Ponte, on this record for asking such a sentence. And then goes on to develop the submission by saying that the Prosecution is acting vindictively and cruelly, simply for maintaining the -- for the accused maintaining his innocence and mounting a vigorous Defence and ends up by saying that if the Prosecution sentencing policy were based on concern for victims you would never see such a disparity. The Prosecution takes exception to any commentary concerning the Office of the Prosecutor or the Prosecutor herself. That sort of commentary was completely and totally uncalled for. It was unnecessary and if I may say, it was a regrettable lack of unlawyerly language. And the Prosecution wishes to state for the purposes of the record the fact that it is most displeased and most upset at that use of language. There are ways and ways, if Your Honours please, of arguing matters in court, ways and ways of making submissions, and language is a good tool for making even the most robust and forceful of submissions without resort to that sort of language and that sort of personal attack. That's what I wanted to say about the matter. I wanted to put it on the record and make it known to this Trial Chamber. If Your Honours please, can we now turn to the actual merits of sentencing in this particular case? I just want to make a few what I'll refer to as bullet points on the issue of the -- how you should look at Deronjic with respect to this particular accused. Don't forget --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

Firstly there was a large number of civilians killed in the village of Glogova and subjected to the risk of being killed, and forcible displacement and deprivation of their property. It was a meticulously planned attack on the village of Glogova in order to facilitate a scheme of creating Serb ethnic territories. The accused in that particular case, in his capacity as president of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bratunac was -- held that position when he actually ordered the attack on the village of Glogova. And you'll find the references to all of those considerations in paragraphs 2 -- 222 of the judgement -- of the sentencing judgement. In that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, would you mind being interrupted by Mr. Jones, Mr. Di Fazio? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I apologise and it's with the greatest regret that do I interrupt but it's essential that I do, particularly since Your Honour has indicated you were sitting on the sentencing judgments. We say that there is a disparity between the ten years requested by the Prosecution and the 18 years requested in our case. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. That's not what I'm saying.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones. Let's not pre-empt the matter because I haven't finished -- I haven't seen the -- heard the conclusion from Mr. Di Fazio. I don't know where he is aiming. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I understood. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll just go on with my submissions, if I may. The Trial Chamber accepted that his guilty plea tends to contribute to the process of reconciliation in Bratunac and in particular in Bosnia-Herzegovina in general, that's paragraph 238. The Trial Chamber concluded that his guilty plea and his readiness to testify in other trials assisted the Tribunal in its search for the truth and prevented historical revisionism. It also spared the victims and witnesses from being required to come and testify. And you'll find that at paragraph 241. So there were significant factors that existed in the case of Mr. Deronjic that had a powerful mitigatory effect that are totally absent here. If Your Honours please. The Trial Chamber referred, and I emphasise this, it's an extremely important matter for Your Honours to consider, it referred to the substantial cooperation of Mr. Deronjic in that particular case. It was unique, he provided unique and corroborative information to the Prosecution, paragraph 246. He appeared in a number of other cases and testified. He appeared and testified in the Momir Nikolic case. He was called by the Trial Chamber in that particular case. He appeared as a witness in the Krstic appeal, in the Blagojevic trial, in the Krajisnik trial, and in the Milosevic trial. He made good on his promises of cooperation and delivered, if Your Honours please, on cooperation. And it's an extremely significant and important factor that you have to consider. And he also provided a large amount of documentation and material to the Prosecution concerning significant Bratunac SDS meetings. He also identified new crimes and perpetrators that had been previously unknown to the Prosecution. And you'll find those references at paragraphs 254 and 255 of the trial judgement. So the Trial Chamber stated that whether it considered all the mitigating circumstances together, and quote giving particular importance to such factors as the guilty plea and substantial cooperation by the accused, a substantial reduction was warranted. Now in this particular case, if Your Honours please, all of that is utterly absent. It's totally absent. First of all there has been no guilty plea. The Defence yesterday referred to examples of the cooperation of Mr. Oric. I believe it referred to the fact that he granted an interview. If Your Honours please, that is not a matter of cooperation. It was a self-serving interview, there was certainly nothing in it that could be remotely considered to be a confession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's one way of putting it. Let's put it like that. MR. DI FAZIO: It is, with respect, if Your Honours please, the -- really the only way of putting it. Don't forget that Your Honours are considering all these things if you find him guilty and if you -- of the charges, of course, and that's the perspective that I'm now speaking to you from. That question still needs to be addressed. It's the question in this case. But I'm now approaching and addressing you on the basis of the position that you have arrived at that conclusion. If having arrived at that conclusion, if having made findings of guilt in respect of these charges, you then look for cooperation, what will you find? You'll find a desert. As far as the interview is concerned that he gave to OTP investigators, it was an interview given as a suspect and as I say, it's entirely self serving and nothing in it can be remotely considered as an admission of guilt, an expression of remorse, an acceptance of the burning and the cruel treatment and the murders that occurred under his watch. Furthermore, the Defence referred to the known signatures of Tedder and Kelly, the two police officers, sorry, the known signatures of the accused were taken by Kelly and Tedder in the course of interviewing him, and the Defence consented to the admission of the declarations of Kelly and Tedder into evidence and that would facilitate the Prosecution in proving its case. That shines a spotlight on how underwhelming the cooperation of the Defence has been in this particular case. They were painted into a corner, if Your Honours please. There was really no realistic or sensible possibility of the Defence being able to challenge the taking of those known signatures. It is breathtaking in its lack of impact as far as cooperation is concerned. And a matter of the -- of almost non-existent impact. Cooperation is striking in its absence in this particular case. And certainly if Your Honours please that other aspect of matters that is so closely tied to cooperation and the guilty plea, expressions of remorse, this entire Defence has been -- the -- there have been no expresses of remorse that you have heard in the trial record, nor in any of the sentencing submissions made by the Defence on behalf of the accused. And so that is also absent. Now, if Mr. Deronjic will not expressed remorse, if he had not cooperated, if he had forced the Prosecution to prove its case, chapter and verse, what would an appropriate -- what appropriate sentence would there have been imposed in that particular case? If you look at it from that point of view, if Your Honours please, a sentence of 18 years' imprisonment sought by the Prosecution is by no means befitting of the terms that I want to use them that have been used by the Defence in describing that range of sentences. So, they are the most significant matters that the Prosecution wants to raise with respect to the -- to the sentencing issues put by the Defence. When you finally -- sorry, there is just one further matter that I should mention in relation to Deronjic and this particular case by way of comparison. And comparisons are, of course, always limited when it comes to sentencing. If Your Honours please, you will know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And they are odious, too. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. If Your Honours please, in this particular case the sentence of 18 years' imprisonment is being sought for six murders, ten individuals who were cruelly treated over extended periods of time, over two separate periods of time, and there were five villages that were destroyed. Five villages and the surrounding communities that were destroyed. Over an extended period of time. Those communities were in the main destroyed forever and the people have not gone back to those villages and resumed their lives. Whole communities have been destroyed. These are extremely serious crimes. In a national jurisdiction you would expect for six murders a sentence of 18 years' imprisonment to be at the bare minimum. If Your Honours please a sentence of 18 years' imprisonment is not excessive. It is not by any means immoderate and it is in the Prosecution's submission utterly appropriate for the crimes that the accused is found guilty of, if that be your finding. They are the submissions that I wanted to make on sentencing. Unless there is anything else I'll move on to the other topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is one point I would like you to elaborate slightly. And that's the point that you have mentioned a couple of minutes ago and which you also referred to in your brief, and that's the question of remorse. What kind of remorse do you have in mind for the purpose of mitigatory factors? MR. DI FAZIO: Expressions of remorse, if Your Honours, please, concerning the cruel treatment that was meted out to the prisoners, expressions of remorse that he did not prevent or punish the perpetrators of the treatment that was meted out to the prisoners. Expressions of remorse for the communities that were destroyed. The houses, the houses of -- and barns of people, simple people who were living up in those areas where the villages were located. Expressions of remorse over those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How would you reconcile that with the accused's presumption of innocence and right to remain silent? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, this jurisdiction requires, often calls for these submissions to be made during the actual trial itself. During the conduct of -- would Your Honours just bear with me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The right of the accused not to incriminate himself basically is what -- I don't I dealt with this myself because that's one part of the Brdjanin judgement that I drafted myself so I dealt with this considerably also because I had an ad hoc submission on it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that basically we have in these trials something which is peculiarly different from ordinary trials in the domestic jurisdiction, where, for example, in my country, and yours, the jurors, the jury, comes with its verdict of guilty or not guilty and if the accused is found guilty in a trial, by jury, then there is a sentencing hearing. It's not always the case, especially not always the case in all jurisdictions, but it is the case in many jurisdictions, including mine so at that point in time if the accused has been found guilty it's no longer incompatible with his presumption of innocence, his right to remain silent, his right not to incriminate himself, to say, yes, now, for the purpose of sentencing, I -- and without prejudice to any right of appeal that I might have I do wish to say how sorry I am that these crimes happened but do you expect the accused to do that in the kind of proceedings that take place before this Tribunal, where there is no sentencing hearing phase at all? This is the issue that I would like to address. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes. Well, no, you wouldn't expect it, if Your Honours please, and furthermore it's going to be rather too late for expressions of remorse to be expressed after conviction. That's the problem. If there had been expresses of remorse from the start, but another sort of defence, a technical Defence or something like that, that might be something that you could take into account. But there has been an absence of any expression of remorse. Certain things are clear. Certain things are clear. It's a difficult question, I know. But certain things are clear. Firstly, you as a -- as the sentencing institution the sentencing body, are permitted to take remorse into account, and you must. You must take it into account because the man who comes here truly remorseful should be given the benefit of any discount that you can afford, that you can afford to give him on -- because of that factor. If there has been none, and there has been none in anything that I've heard, in the time that I've been involved in this case, you can conclude that there is nothing to be -- no downward pressure on the sentence, so to speak, on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to the next point. MR. DI FAZIO: As I said, Your Honours, they are the matters that I wanted to raise with you with respect to sentencing. If Your Honours please, you -- I'll now turn to documents, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, the Trial Chamber, directed a question to me I think Tuesday, concerning how this claim should approach experts who conflict with each other. I've been thinking about it. It's -- I don't know that I can develop much more from what I said to Your Honours the other day. It is, of course, a common -- I'd say it's a very common problem that Tribunals all around the world face. Triers of fact are constantly presented with situations where experts disagree. Examples abound. Wherever there is a defence of intoxication or automatism involving the use of psychiatric evidence to assist the Court in determining the accused's state of mind for a crime that might have occurred under the influence of drugs or alcohol or something like that, for example. Juries in the common law system and Judges in the common law system as well are called upon to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think I may have not made myself understood then. I wasn't worried about that, that I have been doing all my career as a judge. What I was interested in is your legal position when it comes to documents or signatures examined by Professor Bilic and Professor Bilic alone, not by Fagel or Kerzan. And Professor Bilic has come to the conclusion, took the conclusions that he has come to, which on the face of them shed serious doubts on the authenticity of those documents. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.text: Now, short of any evidence, expert evidence, from the Prosecution, short of any expert evidence from the Trial Chamber-appointed expert what is your position, considering that the onus of proof and the authenticity of document rests with you from beginning to end. MR. DI FAZIO: You can see documents that fall into that class outlined immediately in annex B of the Prosecution's submission to its Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. final submission. The -- this issue was A -- was already addressed to a certain extent in the Prosecution final brief, at -- in the Prosecution final brief and addressed in the Defence reply. By that I mean the Prosecution complained in its final brief that the known signatures and known writings of both of those men were not included, not provided, to this Trial Chamber, and then Professor Bilic, using those known signatures and known writings, went on to examine various questioned documents. They are P19, P46, P48, P49, P51, P61, P62, P66, P69, P101, P108, and P485.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget that argument for the time being because that is not exactly what I meant. It's something that obviously we need to deal with, taking into consideration your submissions and also the submissions of the Defence. What I am asking you to direct your attention at is the following: Forgetting that argument, forgetting that submission completely, we do have, as the state of affairs an expert's report which in so many words tells us exhibits 1, 2, 3, 4, are not authentic in my opinion because I have examined the signature with what I had and I have come to that conclusion on the basis of my expertise. Okay? We can't control that. You could have controlled that because the Prosecution -- the Defence has submitted that you were put on notice from the beginning of the trial that all these documents were challenged, and the submission is if they could get hold of Fejzic and get his specimen signatures then you could have done the same. If they could manage to find signatures of Salihovic, you could have found the same, just as you tried to do with Dzananovic signature. This is the argument but again forget that. The state of affairs, the status quo, is now, not as the status question and/or any other status quo, the status quo is there is an expert's report by an expert chosen by the Defence who says, These are my findings. Are those findings in your opinion contradicted in any way by any much your evidence to start with? This is the basic point that you need to address. If they are in your opinion, could you please come forward and tell us how they are? And if they are not, if they are not, specifically contradicted, then what is your position as regards the onus of proof that you have throughout the proceedings of proving the authenticity of those documents keeping in mind that the Defence need only, if they decide to challenge, they don't have the onus of proving the non-authenticity or the forgery of those documents. They only have a -- not even a burden, a responsibility to show what they tried to show, and whatever they need to indicate to us can be satisfied on the basis of probabilities only and not on beyond a reasonable doubt, as you have. I don't know if I have made myself clear. If I haven't, please do tell me and I will try and explain again. MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honour has made yourself very clear. There is no -- I understand perfectly. The last issue -- I can instantly answer. The Prosecution bears its burden throughout. It's got it on its shoulders now, and it will have it on its shoulders at the time you're writing your judgement and it had it at the time before the trial started. We never lose it. It always remains and never transfers to the Defence except in the most odd circumstances that don't apply in this case at all. So that's -- that is the Prosecution position. We accept that. Now, as far as other evidence that might assist you in weighing up Professor Bilic's evidence, is concerned, the Prosecution can only point you to these two main features. Firstly the authors, as far as the Salihovic signatures are concerned, of course with the Fejzic signatures, you've got the other -- the juxtaposition of the Oric signature and the Fejzic signature. So that is something that you can consider in assessing, weighing up, what Professor Bilic says about the falsity of these documents or what the Prosecution says to you about the reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What would be your best scenario and your worst scenario in relation to the Salihovic signatures or alleged signatures? MR. DI FAZIO: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The best and worst scenario. I mean -- MR. DI FAZIO: Worst case scenario is you accept everything that Professor Bilic says and find that what he says might possibly or reasonably be true and it casts doubt upon your acceptance of the documents as reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think it's fair enough. Let's -- MR. DI FAZIO: I hope I didn't mix my words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I understood you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I just don't want to leave that other point. The one that Your Honours say you have understood. It's regarding the failure to provide known signatures and known writings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't take me wrong. I didn't criticise you for that. I was repeating the arguments put by the Defence in your regard on that. I wasn't at all commenting. MR. DI FAZIO: It's a feature of the evidence that in the Prosecution's submission compels you to ignore the evidence of Bilic in so far as the Fejzic and the Salihovic signatures are concerned. And as far as the Fejzic signatures are concerned, it's all of the evidence there should lead to you have very serious doubts about the reliability of Professor Bilic. If I can use -- just make an analogy that's going to be I think will demonstrate my point, on the -- what I say are the devastating consequences of the failure to provide those known signatures and writings, the only way an expert comes along not to give evidence of fact but to give you his opinions, which he's permitted to do because he's an expert and that's an exception to the normal rule. So in order for you to weigh up, judge, consider his opinions that he expresses here in the witness box, you've got to know what foundation they are built on. You must know that, because otherwise you can't judge it. And the tool for the Prosecution to do that is through cross-examination. Now the Prosecution was deprived of any chance, any chance, to attack these particular conclusions concerning Salihovic and Fejzic. You will never know on what it's based, just as the Prosecution doesn't know. If you don't have the known writings, you can't -- you can't see the -- can't assess the foundation that the expert builds his opinion on. If the police find a man who has been shot and two blocks away they find the man with the gun and they think that that's the killer, and they take the gun and the man and they take him down to the police station and they say, We think you're a murderer and this is your gun that you used to kill someone. And they conduct an autopsy on the body and they extract the bullet. They get the bullet and they take it off to their analyst and they this is the bullet that comes from the dead man and this is the gun that we think was used to fire it. And the analyst goes ahead and he hits his gun and he fires six shots and he analyses the bullets and he looks at the stripes and the striations and the patterns and so forth on the bullets, and then he comes along and he says, No doubt about it. That's -- that gun fired that one bullet that landed in the dead man's body and it also fired the six other bullets that I saw and I tested. Then how do you expect Prosecution or defence, depending on who is adducing that evidence to test it, if they don't have the six bullets? How does it work? Where do you start? I can't -- I can't offer you any assistance on Salihovic, on what Professor Bilic said about the Salihovic and Fejzic signatures because I can't test, I couldn't -- or rather Mr. Wubben couldn't test Professor Bilic. How do I approach it? And that failure is catastrophic for that section of Professor Bilic's evidence. The Defence in its reply said, oh, well you know, it's -- you go to -- it's -- it's nothing to do with Professor Bilic. It was a decision of counsel. It doesn't matter whose decision it was. If the foundation -- you can't see what the foundation is made of, you can't judge the opinion. And so for that reason, that's the end of the Salihovic and the Fejzic evidence, as far as Bilic is -- Professor Bilic is concerned. If Your Honours please, the Dzanan Dzananovic, did you want to hear me on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, of course. I mean, I did put it to you on Tuesday or Monday. MR. DI FAZIO: I won't be long. If Your Honours please, here we have clear evidence that some documents that the Prosecution has produced to you don't -- do not bear the Dzananovic signature. Someone else wrote the Dzananovic signature. Madam Vidovic made the submission to you, I think it was Madam Vidovic, on -- at page 16362, she referred to two documents, I believe, P17, P333. The -- there is a -- the expert report of Dr. Fagel is not in evidence, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, concerning all of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's been put in evidence by the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. The Dzananovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. That solves my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But then it deals also with a number of other documents that were shown to him. And what we did, we checked then with the other document that has been tendered by the Defence, which is Dr. Fagel's report to you dealing with several documents that were handed to him supposedly containing the signature of Dzananovic. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the highest is probably not. MR. DI FAZIO: I know that. What -- I wasn't concerned about that. I wanted to highlight that, in fact, but I wasn't sure it was in evidence and I didn't want to -- giving evidence from the bar table.

utterances.text: My concern, Mr. Di Fazio, is that in that situation you're still making use of P15, P16, P17, these are all the same genre of documents, of reports, supposedly of the military police et cetera. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point is this: Let's start with P15. P15 is the one which was dealt specifically with by both Dzananovic in his statement to the OTP. He saw the document ending with 9558, the last four numbers, last four digits, and he said, "That is definitely not my signature." MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, P15, P16, P17, and P18 are all Dzananovic documents which were examined together with a whole list of other documents by Professor -- by Dr. Fagel, your expert, for you, exclusively for the office of the -- and he has come to the conclusion, one or the others, that these are either definitely not the signature of Dzananovic or probably not the signature of Dzananovic. In the case of 15, his finding would obviously strengthen the position of Dzananovic when he affirms that that is not his signature. P15 you made use of during the proceedings, during the hearings. You made use of it with more than one witness. P16, P17, and P18, you did not refer to any witness, but you still rely on these four exhibits in your final brief. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes.

Question to him, to Mr. Ivanovic, was: Did there come a point in time that you were removed from the cell and taken to another room in this building to be questioned? The answer: Yes. I remember once, I can't say whether it was more than that. They took me to the reception room where they had the soldiers who watched us. I was taken out of the room and taken to the reception room. utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would like to go over one legal point. I'd like to emphasise and possibly, Your Honours might consider just re-emphasising certain points concerning necessity as a defence. Military necessity, military object, and then military advantage. Necessity as a defence. Your Honours have already set forth in their Rule 98 bis decision that necessity can be a defence when an act that is criminal has occurred and Your Honours referred to that as it concerned the plunder counts which were dropped, and the seeking and pillaging of food. Those criminal acts were excused by necessity. The Defence would want to conflate that necessity and military necessity. Military necessity is quite a different thing. Military necessity only exists when they have clearly identified a military object and during an attack one is going after a military object, and destruction that occurs could be part of what is under military necessity. One does not go to military necessity first for wanton destruction and then fall back and say, oh, that was a military object. One has to be clear that what was attacked was a military object and not a civilian object, such as an entire village, an entire town. The Defence in their closing arguments talk about military advantage. If an area gives them a military advantage, well, Your Honour, a military advantage in and of itself still has to be qualified by the military objective, how the attack is carried out after identifying the military advantage that might be a military objective is still measured by military necessity. One has to look at the nature, location, and purpose, and to see whether the area is making an effective contribution to military action and whose destruction offers a definite military advantage. The Defence's notion is much more generalised, that towns and areas and villages offered a military advantage. Your Honours have to look at international humanitarian law with the safeguards that it's set up to provide. Now, it's possible that the rocket launcher in a town is legitimate military object and then one will see the destruction that occurred in going after the rocket launcher covered by military necessity and the taking out of that rocket launcher might be in and of itself a military advantage but a military advantage because a rocket launcher was making an effective contribution to military action. That is how Your Honours will have to look at the application of humanitarian law to the situations that you were being asked to evaluate. And that is an application that holds for all sides, all parties. Just as the lobbing in of rockets or launchers into the town of Srebrenica without distinguishing, without making a distinction between a military object that might be the Domavija Hotel because soldiers are billeted there or the PTT building because it's a military headquarter. Lobbing guns -- I'm sorry, bombs or weapons into all of Srebrenica because it might offer a military advantage to the Serbs is illegal. The illegality of that was certainly felt and suffered by the people in Srebrenica. This Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor, and Your Honours are not looking for political parity. You're looking for the just application of the law. Your Honours, I was going to address issues of in essence perfidy, when a civilian is really a combatant. There are many small things that have come up. Let it please be known that the Office of the Prosecutor is in no way saying that people who are in civilian clothing are per se trying to fool and become war criminals. I believe that our reference even to paragraph 114 of the Blaskic appeal sets that notion aside. And there are many other small things that the Prosecutor could have answered. The 13 questions that the Defence raised, some of those outright are just positions of the Prosecution, they are not errors. Some might have been very small errors, misreading of sentences. I'll let Your Honours be the judge of that because I think the evidence reveals that. I'd like to close by saying the following: "The Defence raised I think a very good observation. Nedjeljko Radic said, I want Kemo. I would feel happier if Kemo was here." The Prosecution agrees, Kemo, if tried, is also probably a war criminal. But this Tribunal was set up so that the Kemos don't even get near the prisoners, so that those in positions of superior authority, prevent the Kemos from being able to undertake those criminal acts. And when Kemo wasn't prevented, Kemo is to be punished and if the superior, the military superior of Kemo, doesn't undertake his duties, and he knew or had reason to know, then it is that superior that is liable and that's how we protect victims of all sides of the conflicts, Your Honour. Those are the submissions of the Prosecution, prior to you undertaking your solemn duty.
